--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.average_degree_connectivity()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: >- Get the average neighbor degree of nodes, grouped by their own degree. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.average_degree_connectivity()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: >- Get the average neighbor degree of nodes, grouped by their own degree. title: >- [Graph.average_degree_connectivity()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: >- Get the average neighbor degree of nodes, grouped by their own degree. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get the average neighbor degree of nodes, grouped by their own degree. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L37462-L37563){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.average_degree_connectivity( source_mode="in+out", target_mode="in+out", weighted=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Average degree connectivity](../assets/graphs/average-degree-connectivity.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Two hubs C and D of degree 3, linked to each other and to two leaves of degree 1 apiece. Every leaf's neighbor is a hub, so degree 1 maps to 3.0, while the hubs' six neighbors have degrees 1, 1, 3, 3, 1, 1, so degree 3 maps to 1.667: a falling curve, the mark of disassortative mixing." width="100%"} For each degree `k`, the average degree of the neighbors of all nodes with degree `k`, often written `k_nn(k)`. Plotted against `k`, it shows the network's degree mixing at a glance: a rising curve means high-degree nodes link to each other (assortative, as in many social networks), a falling curve means hubs link to low-degree nodes (disassortative, as in many technological and biological networks). It is the degree-resolved version of `assortativity_degree()` and the aggregate of `average_neighbor_degree()`. With weights, each neighbor's degree counts in proportion to the weight of the edge to it. Values match NetworkX's `average_degree_connectivity()`, except on directed graphs with `source_mode="in+out"`: NetworkX's documentation describes in- and out-neighbors, but its code averages over successors only while dividing by the total degree. EdgeCase follows the documented definition, counting every incident edge. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source_mode]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["in+out"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : On directed graphs, which neighbors to average over and which degree groups nodes: `"out"` (successors, by out-degree), `"in"` (predecessors, by in-degree), or `"in+out"` (default, all neighbors, by total degree). [target_mode]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["in+out"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : On directed graphs, which degree of the neighbors to average: `"in"`, `"out"`, or `"in+out"` (default). [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to weight by edge weight. If `None` (default), follows the graph. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, float]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A dictionary mapping each degree `k` present in the graph to the average degree of those nodes' neighbors, sorted by `k`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `source_mode=` or `target_mode=` is invalid, or set to something other than `"in+out"` on an undirected graph. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~average_neighbor_degree`) : The average degree of each node's neighbors. [](`~assortativity_degree`) : One number for the same tendency. [](`~degree_mixing_dict`) : Count links by the degrees at their two ends. ## Examples {.doc-examples} `C` and `D` have three neighbors each, and `A`, `B`, `E` and `F` one. Each node with one neighbor is joined to a node with three, while the neighbors of `C` and `D` have `1 + 1 + 3` neighbors between them, `5 / 3` on average: ::: {#48077253 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("A", "C"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("D", "F")] ) graph.average_degree_connectivity() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {1: 3.0, 3: 1.6666666666666667} ``` ::: ::: ### Friends of the well connected `karate_club()` links the 34 members of a university karate club who met outside the club, before it split in two. Member `11` has one friend, the instructor, who has 16. The more friends members have, the fewer their friends have, falling to under 4 for the administrator, who has 17: ::: {#05911c16 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} karate = ec.karate_club() knn = karate.average_degree_connectivity() {k: round(v, 1) for k, v in knn.items()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {1: 16.0, 2: 12.4, 3: 8.2, 4: 8.5, 5: 10.5, 6: 8.3, 9: 5.8, 10: 6.6, 12: 5.1, 16: 4.3, 17: 3.8} ``` ::: ::: Colored by the average number of friends their friends have, the members on the edge of the club are the darkest: ::: {#b8ef96f4 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} karate = karate.average_neighbor_degree() karate.plot( color_by="average_neighbor_degree", size_by="degree", label_by="label", seed=1, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
